guideTitle: 6 Best Medical Alert Systems Under $100 in 2026
metaDescription: Six alert pendants and call-button kits compared on where alerts go, fall detection, GPS and range, to help you choose a setup that fits your household.
introParagraphs: A larger budget ceiling for a personal alert device makes one new option realistic: a pendant that sends alerts directly to family members instead of a call center. Alongside it you still find monitored pendants, a cellular GPS unit and plain in-home call buttons, and the right choice depends on who will actually answer.

The six picks here span three designs. SecuLife is a family-alert pendant with GPS and fall detection, the Medical Guardian MGMini and Bay Alarm Medical device connect to professional monitoring, and the PRNBRH, STECHRO and CallToU kits use home radio or Wi-Fi to ring a person nearby. We evaluated listing details and described features only.
Nothing here is a promise of rescue. Ask who gets the alert, what ongoing terms apply, and how the device behaves out of range before you buy.

products.name: SecuLife Medical Alert Pendant with Fall Detection and GPS
products.description:
The SecuLife is a wearable pendant that sends alerts straight to chosen family contacts instead of a staffed monitoring center. The listing describes automatic fall detection that works without a button press, GPS location, and an SOS button that places a cellular call, with two-way calling. A monthly subscription is mentioned on the listing, so read the plan details before ordering.

The design makes sense for families who want to be the first responders. Alerts reach people who know the wearer and their medical history, which can save time explaining. The flip side is that nobody trained is on the line, so if family members do not answer, there is no fallback team.

In this lineup it is the only pendant that combines family routing, fall detection and GPS. Compared with the MGMini, it skips the call center. Compared with the Bay Alarm Medical device, it takes a different approach to who responds. It suits families who are reliably reachable and willing to act as the responders.
products.bestFor: Families who want to receive alerts directly and know the wearer's routines.
pros: Alerts reach family contacts without a call center
Automatic fall detection needs no button press
GPS location is part of the feature set
SOS button supports two-way calling
cons: No professional team stands behind the alerts
A monthly subscription is mentioned on the listing
GPS accuracy and battery life need checking

products.name: Medical Guardian MGMini Alert Necklace, Pearl or Silver
products.description:
The MGMini is a small necklace-style alert device that connects to the maker's 24/7 monitoring team. Press the button, speak through the built-in two-way speaker and the team responds. The product page says monitoring must be activated online or by phone before first use, and that a subscription is required.

The finish options, including Silver, Pearl and Rose Gold, make it look more like jewelry than medical equipment, which matters for people who dislike wearing something obvious. The tradeoff is that the device alone does nothing until service is active, so budget time for setup. The listing we reviewed does not describe fall detection.

Compared with the SecuLife, it brings a trained team into the loop but lacks the family-routing option. Compared with the pager kits, it leaves the house with you. It is the choice for someone who wants a staffed monitoring service in an unobtrusive form.
products.bestFor: Wearers who want a discreet pendant backed by a staffed monitoring team.
pros: Pendant look is discreet enough to wear daily
Two-way speaker links to a monitoring team
Several finishes to match personal style
Service activation can be done by phone
cons: Does nothing until a service plan is active
Fall detection is not on the listing

products.name: Bay Alarm Medical SOS Mobile GPS, 4G Medical Alert
products.description:
The Bay Alarm Medical SOS Mobile is a portable 4G LTE device with GPS and optional fall detection, and it does not require a landline. The listing notes that a subscription is required for full functionality and that activation is by phone. It advertises nationwide cellular connectivity for use away from home.

Portability is the story. If the wearer gardens, walks, shops or travels, a unit that follows them is more useful than a base station that only covers the house. The tradeoff is that a mobile plan generally costs more than a home-only system, and coverage depends on the cellular network at each location.

Compared with the SecuLife, it routes alerts through a monitoring service rather than directly to family. Compared with the MGMini, it adds GPS and an optional fall feature. It is the stronger fit for active people who spend much of the day outside the house.
products.bestFor: Active wearers who need protection away from home and prefer a monitored service.
pros: Portable 4G unit works outside the house
GPS location is a listed feature
No landline is needed in the home
Fall detection can be added as an option
cons: Mobile plans usually cost more than home-only ones
Coverage depends on local cellular reception

products.name: PRNBRH Wi-Fi Alert System with 2 Call Buttons
products.description:
The PRNBRH kit offers a waterproof wrist remote, call buttons and phone-app control, and the listing says there is no monthly fee. It connects through Wi-Fi and a separate wireless signal, so a press can reach the base even if one path has trouble. It also mentions fall alert functionality that notifies a connected phone.

It works best as a household tool. A press triggers a local alarm and a notification to a phone, so help depends on a family member or neighbor nearby. That makes it a sensible low-ongoing-cost choice for a shared home, and a weaker one for somebody living alone.

In comparison with the pagers, it adds a phone app and a wrist remote. In comparison with the SecuLife, it works only near the base, not on a walk. Confirm how the fall alert is triggered and what it requires before counting on that feature.
products.bestFor: Shared homes where someone is usually around to answer an app alert.
pros: No monthly fee is stated on the listing
Waterproof wrist remote for showers
Phone app control and push alerts
Uses Wi-Fi plus a separate wireless signal
cons: Alerts reach a phone, not a call center

products.name: STECHRO Wireless Caregiver Pager, Expandable System
products.description:
The STECHRO is a one-button, one-receiver wireless pager with a stated range of up to 1500 ft, 58 ringtones and five volume levels reaching 120 dB. The maker says you can expand it with extra buttons or receivers. There is no app or monitoring service in the listing, just a button and a loud receiver.

That plainness is the benefit. Older adults who do not use smartphones, and caregivers who want a reliable alarm in a bedroom or kitchen, can use it with no Wi-Fi setup. The limit is that the only alert is at the receiver, so it needs a person to be within hearing distance.

Against the CallToU, the STECHRO states a longer range and a higher maximum volume. Against the PRNBRH, it lacks a phone app. Range numbers are usually quoted in open air, so test it inside your home before relying on it.
products.bestFor: Caregivers who want a plain, loud receiver with expansion options.
pros: Stated range reaches up to 1500 ft
Volume levels climb as high as 120 dB
Additional buttons or receivers can be added
No app or Wi-Fi setup is needed
cons: Alerts only sound at the receiver
No phone notification option is described

products.name: CallToU Caregiver Pager Wireless Call Button System
products.description:
The CallToU pairs one call button with one portable receiver, with a stated open-area range of 500 ft or more, 55 ringtones and five volume levels up to 110 dB. The receiver is designed to be carried, so a caregiver can take it to a bedroom, kitchen or garden. The listing positions it for home care and residents who need to call for help.

Portability is the distinguishing feature. A caregiver does not have to stay beside a base station, and the receiver can follow them around the house. The tradeoff is a shorter stated range than the STECHRO and no app, so a person away from the receiver will not hear it.

Compared with the STECHRO at 1500 ft, it covers less distance but is built around carrying. Compared with the PRNBRH, it has no phone app or wrist remote. It is a simple, inexpensive style of alert for a caregiver who moves around the house.
products.bestFor: Caregivers who move between rooms and want to carry the receiver.

Fifty-five ringtone choices and five volumes
Open-area range listed at 500 ft or more
No subscription or app is described

buyingCriteria.explanation: The most important question is who responds. Pendants like the MGMini route to a staffed team, the SecuLife routes to family, and the PRNBRH, STECHRO and CallToU ring a nearby person. If no one is reliably available, choose a monitored service. Ask what happens when an alert goes unanswered.

A pendant with a cellular radio needs a service plan, and the hardware alone may do nothing. The MGMini requires activation before first use, the Bay Alarm Medical device activates by phone, and the SecuLife lists a monthly plan. Read terms for cancellation, coverage and what happens if payments stop.

Automatic fall detection can summon help when a person cannot press a button, but it can also miss events or fire falsely. The SecuLife lists it as automatic, and the Bay Alarm Medical device lists it as optional. Treat any fall feature as a backup to the button, never a replacement.

GPS and cellular coverage allow a device to work outdoors, while home-based pagers do not. If the wearer leaves the house often, favor the SecuLife or the Bay Alarm Medical device. For people who stay home, the PRNBRH, STECHRO or CallToU may be enough.

For pagers, ranges quoted in open air shrink through walls and floors. The STECHRO states 1500 ft and the CallToU states 500 ft or more. Test in your own layout and aim for a volume you can hear from the farthest room.

A device that is not worn cannot help. Choose a form the user will wear in the shower and overnight, such as the PRNBRH waterproof wrist remote or the MGMini necklace. Confirm waterproof claims on the listing and test the button after it gets wet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Alert routing
howWeEvaluated.description: We grouped each product by where alerts go: family for the SecuLife, a staffed team for the MGMini and Bay Alarm Medical device, and nearby people for the PRNBRH, STECHRO and CallToU. This shaped the ranking more than any feature.

howWeEvaluated.title: Service and setup terms
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked what each listing says about activation, subscriptions and fees. The MGMini and Bay Alarm Medical device need plans, the SecuLife mentions a monthly subscription, and the pagers describe none. We did not assume terms that were not stated.

howWeEvaluated.title: Detection and location features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for fall detection, GPS and two-way calling. The SecuLife combines all three, the Bay Alarm Medical device has GPS and optional fall detection, and the MGMini has a two-way speaker. The pagers have none of these.

howWeEvaluated.title: Range and volume
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated range and alarm volume for the radio kits. The STECHRO leads with 1500 ft and 120 dB, the CallToU states 500 ft or more and 110 dB, and the PRNBRH relies on Wi-Fi and a wireless signal. All figures are best-case.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The SecuLife is the family-routing pick, the MGMini is the discreet monitored pick, the Bay Alarm Medical device is the mobile pick, the PRNBRH is the app pick, the STECHRO is the range pick and the CallToU is the portable-receiver pick.

faq.q: Is a family-alert pendant safer than a monitored one?
faq.a: Neither is a guarantee. The SecuLife reaches family directly, which can be quick if they answer, while the MGMini reaches a staffed team. Think about who is realistically reachable at different hours and choose accordingly.

faq.q: Do I have to pay every month?
faq.a: The MGMini and Bay Alarm Medical device require a subscription, and the SecuLife listing mentions a monthly plan. The PRNBRH, STECHRO and CallToU describe no monitoring fee. Check the plan page for current terms before buying.

faq.q: Can a pager replace a monitored device?
faq.a: No, because pagers only alert someone nearby. If the wearer is alone, there may be no one to hear it. A monitored device or a family-routed pendant is a better fit for people living alone.

faq.q: How reliable is automatic fall detection?
faq.a: It is a helpful extra, but it can miss falls or fire when none occurred. The SecuLife lists it as automatic and the Bay Alarm Medical device as optional. Encourage the wearer to press the button whenever possible. Also remind them that a pendant tucked under heavy clothing or left on a nightstand cannot sense a fall, so consistent daily wear matters as much as the feature list.

faq.q: What if the user goes outside the house?
faq.a: Home pagers stop working beyond their range. Cellular devices such as the SecuLife and Bay Alarm Medical SOS Mobile use GPS and mobile networks. Check cellular coverage in the areas the wearer visits.

faq.q: How do I check range before relying on a pager?
faq.a: Place the receiver where the caregiver spends time, then press the button from the farthest rooms. Open-air figures like 1500 ft on the STECHRO fall with walls and floors. Repeat the test after moving furniture or changing routines. If a room is a dead spot, move the receiver to a more central position, or add a second receiver if the system allows it, as the STECHRO states it does.

faq.q: Should I talk to a clinician about which device to choose?
faq.a: It can help, particularly if the wearer has specific mobility or health needs. These listings describe features, not medical outcomes. A care team can advise on how much support is appropriate. Bring the specific listing details to that conversation, including the alert path, plan terms and range, so the advice matches the product you are actually considering.
